- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–15% to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤-0.3) and forecast is overly conservative, slightly increase the low-end of the range to avoid underestimating rebound.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history show strong downward momentum, model tends to overcorrect — apply a downward bias correction of 2–5% to the forecast mean.  
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (±0.3), model often overestimates volatility — cap forecast range width at 10% of recent 7-day average volatility.  
- If forecast shows a sharp upward move followed by a steep drop (e.g., spike then collapse), reduce the subsequent drop by 10–20% to avoid “overshoot after spike” bias.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history are trending upward, model tends to overestimate continuation — apply a downward adjustment of 3–8% to the forecast mean.  
- If sentiment is consistently positive over 5+ days, model tends to overestimate future highs — apply a 5–10% downward correction to the forecast peak.  
- If sentiment is consistently negative over 5+ days, model tends to underestimate future lows — apply a 5–10% upward correction to the forecast trough.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history show high volatility, reduce forecast variance by 20–30% to avoid overfitting to noise.  
- If forecast is significantly above true outcome for 3 consecutive days, apply a “mean reversion” correction: subtract 1–3% from the next forecast to align with recent trend.  
- If forecast is significantly below true outcome for 3 consecutive days, apply a “mean reversion” correction: add 1–3% to the next forecast to align with recent trend.
